content: Rigor, also known as shaking chills or shivering, refers to the sensation of feeling cold, often accompanied by involuntary muscle contractions. The term chills may also describe episodes of shivering, which are often associated with paleness and a subjective feeling of coldness. Goosebumps, while sometimes associated with a sensation of chilliness, are not necessarily linked to chills or fever. Goosebumps occur when the body raises its hairs to create an insulating layer. Chills, on the other hand, are caused by rapid muscle contractions and relaxations, which generate heat when the body perceives itself as cold. These episodes often signal the onset of a fever or an increase in the body’s core temperature. Chills can also be a significant and consistent symptom in certain diseases, such as malaria. Chills are particularly common in young children, who tend to develop higher fevers than adults, even in response to minor illnesses. Infants, however, may not exhibit obvious chills. Any fever in an infant younger than six months should be reported to a healthcare provider. Similarly, fevers in infants aged six months to one year should be reported unless the cause is definitively known. Causes of Rigor Rigor can result from various causes, including: Viral and bacterial infections, such as: Bacterial gastroenteritis. Common colds. Infectious mononucleosis. Influenza. Meningitis. Pneumonia. Strep throat. Viral gastroenteritis. Urinary tract infections, such as pyelonephritis. Diagnosis To diagnose the cause of rigor, a healthcare provider will take a detailed medical history and perform a physical examination. Questions may include: Diagnostic tests may include: Blood tests, such as a complete blood count (CBC) or blood differential. Urinalysis. Blood cultures. Sputum cultures. Urine cultures. Chest X-rays. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care Immediate medical attention is necessary if: There is neck stiffness, confusion, significant irritability, or lethargy. There is a severe cough, shortness of breath, abdominal pain, or burning/frequent urination. A child younger than three months has a temperature of 101°F (38.3°C) or higher. A child aged three months to one year has a fever lasting more than 24 hours. A fever remains above 103°F (39.4°C) after 1–2 hours of home treatment. A fever does not improve after three days or persists for more than five days. Infants younger than six months rarely exhibit obvious chills, but any fever in this age group should be reported to a healthcare provider. Fevers in infants aged six months to one year should also be reported unless the cause is definitively known. Treatment Options Treatment for rigor depends on the duration and severity of the chills and any accompanying symptoms, particularly fever. Home Care Fever, which often accompanies chills, is the body’s natural response to various conditions, such as infections. If the fever is mild (102°F or lower) and there are no concerning side effects, professional treatment may not be necessary. Recommended home care includes: Drinking plenty of fluids and getting adequate rest. Using evaporation to cool the skin and reduce body temperature. Sponging with warm water (approximately 70°F) may help lower a fever. Avoid cold water, as it can be uncomfortable and may trigger chills, potentially worsening the fever. Taking medications such as acetaminophen to reduce fever and chills. Avoiding bundling up in blankets, as this can raise body temperature further. Home Care for Children For children with a temperature over 102°F or who appear uncomfortable, pain-relieving medications such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen can be administered. Always follow the recommended dosage on the medication label. Aspirin should not be given to children with viral symptoms due to the risk of Reye syndrome. If a child’s temperature exceeds 103.5°F after 1–2 hours of fever-reducing medication, place the child in a tub of lukewarm water up to the navel. Use a wet washcloth or towel to gently rub the child’s body for 20 minutes or as long as tolerated. Add warm water as needed to maintain a constant water temperature and prevent shivering. Afterward, pat the child dry with a towel (do not rub), dress them in light clothing, provide fluids, and keep the room cool but comfortable. Avoid using ice water or rubbing alcohol to reduce a child’s temperature, as these methods can cause shock. Do not bundle a feverish child in blankets, and do not wake a sleeping child to administer medication or take their temperature, as sleep is more beneficial.
